text: Fleabag is a British comedy-drama television series created and written by Phoebe Waller-Bridge, adapted from her 2013 Edinburgh Festival Fringe one-woman play of the same name, which won a Fringe First Award. The series was produced by Two Brothers Pictures for BBC Three and co-produced with Amazon Studios. Waller-Bridge stars as Fleabag, a free-spirited but angry and confused young woman living in London, while Sian Clifford co-stars as her sister Claire, and Andrew Scott joins in the second season; most main characters are unnamed, including Waller-Bridge and Scott. The protagonist frequently breaks the fourth wall, delivering exposition, internal monologues, and commentary to the audience. The show premiered on 21 July 2016 and concluded its second and final series on 8 April 2019. It received widespread critical acclaim for its writing, acting, and the unique personality of the title character, with many critics and viewers calling it one of the greatest comedy and television series of all time. Waller-Bridge won the British Academy Television Award for Best Female Comedy Performance for the first series, and the second series earned her Primetime Emmy Awards for Outstanding Comedy Series, Outstanding Lead Actress, and Outstanding Writing for a Comedy Series; additional acting nominations were given to Clifford, Olivia Colman, Fiona Shaw, and Kristin Scott Thomas. The series also won the Golden Globe Awards for Best Television Series and Best Actress for Waller-Bridge, with a nomination for Scott. The initial concept for Fleabag came from a challenge by a friend to create a 10-minute sketch for a stand-up storytelling night. BBC Three originally broadcast the show, with a repeat run on BBC Two from 21 August to 25 September 2016; the second series aired simultaneously on BBC One and BBC Three, with BBC Three only offering it online. The show was picked up by Amazon Prime Video and premiered in the United States on 16 September 2016, with Series 2 released on 17 May 2019; it is also available on IFC in the US and Net5 in the Netherlands. A French remake titled Mouche (meaning 'fly') was produced by Jeanne Herry and aired on 3 June 2019 on Canal+, set in Paris with Camille Cottin in the lead role. Filming took place in and around London, primarily in North West and Central areas, with key locations including Dartmouth Park, Southampton Road, Laurier Road, Croftdown Road, Highgate Road, York Rise, Twickenham, Hampton Hill, Highgate, Tufnell Park, Belsize Park, Maida Vale, Kentish Town, Parliament Hill Fields, Southwark, Bloomsbury, Soho, Stanmore, Lincoln's Inn Fields, and Finsbury Square. Specific sets include Bold Café & Restaurant in Dartmouth Park as Fleabag's Guinea Pig Café, Cambridge Park Road in Twickenham for Dad and Godmother's house, the British Museum's Lecture Theatre in Russell Square for the feminist lecture, Kensal Green Cemetery for the daily jog, Hedsor House in Maidenhead for the silent retreat, Smith & Wollensky in Covent Garden for the family dinner party, St. Andrew's in Kingsbury for Hot Priest's church, the Tate Modern in Bankside for Godmother's sexhibition, Heron Tower in Bishopsgate for Claire's penthouse office, St Dunstan and All Saints Church in Stepney for the funeral, and 137 – Taylor and Taylor in Shoreditch for the hair salon. Filming for the first series began in late April 2016 and aired from 21 July to 25 August 2016; filming for the second series started in late August 2018 and aired from 4 March to 8 April 2019. Isobel Waller-Bridge, Phoebe's sister, composed the music for both series. Both series received 100% approval ratings on Rotten Tomatoes, with the first averaging 8.5/10 based on 42 reviews and the second 9.3/10 based on 99 reviews; Metacritic awarded the first series a score of 88 out of 100 and the second 96 out of 100, both indicating universal acclaim. Critics such as Emily Nussbaum of The New Yorker described the first series as a "precision black-humour mechanism, a warped and affecting fable about one single woman's existence," Maureen Ryan of Variety called it "scathingly funny" and noted it reveals itself as a tragedy, Hank Stuever of The Washington Post described it as a "funny, highly profane but surprisingly poignant dramedy," Mike Hale of The New York Times praised its "restless, almost feral energy and its slap-in-the-face attitude," and Mary McNamara of the Los Angeles Times commended its unpredictability and "clear eye for truth that often becomes, like all good comedy, quite devastating." The second series received unanimous acclaim and was considered a cultural phenomenon, with Serena Davies of The Daily Telegraph calling it "a near-perfect work of art," Mary Elizabeth Williams of Salon praising it as a "brilliant swan song," Alan Sepinwall of Rolling Stone calling it a "tragicomic masterpiece reaching new heights," James Poniewozik of The New York Times noting it feels "immediately confident, if inevitably less groundbreaking" but continues to push its form, and Hannah Jane Parkinson of The Guardian describing the conclusion as "the most electrifying, devastating TV in years," stating that many who did not watch or appreciate the first series were converted. Fleabag was ranked second-highest among shows of the 2010s by Metacritic's decade-end list and has since been recognized by multiple publications as one of the greatest television series of all time. Former U.S. President Barack Obama named the second season among his favorite films and television series of 2019, including it in his annual list on Twitter on 29 December 2019 with the addendum: "and a quick list of TV shows that I considered as powerful as movies: Fleabag: Season 2, Unbelievable, and Watchmen."
